segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to the earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the abyss.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He opened the shaft of the abyss, and smoke rose from the shaft like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the shaft.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Out of the smoke locusts came onto the earth, and they were given power like the power that the scorpions of the earth have.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only the people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were not permitted to kill them, but only to torment them for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a person.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days people will seek death and will never find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The locusts looked like horses prepared for battle. On their heads were what seemed to be crowns like gold, and their faces were like human faces,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots with many horses rushing into battle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have tails like scorpions, and stingers, and in their tails is their power to harm people for five months.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have as king over them the angel of the abyss; his name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he has the name Apollyon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first woe has passed. Look, two more woes are still coming after this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the horns of the golden altar that is before God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to the sixth angel, the one who had the trumpet,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the four angels were released, who had been kept ready for the hour and day and month and year, to kill a third of humankind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The number of the cavalry troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is how I saw the horses in the vision, and those seated on them: they wore breastplates of fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow. The heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and out of their mouths came fire and smoke and sulfur.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed—by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur that came out of their mouths.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like snakes, with heads, and with them they do harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The rest of humankind, those who were not killed by these plagues, still did not turn back from the works of their hands, so as to stop worshiping demons and the idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they did not turn back from their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

notes.note: The Greek tense shows that John does not watch the star fall; he sees it already fallen. The star is treated as a personal being who receives a key and opens the shaft, in keeping with the Jewish habit of picturing angels as stars. Whether this figure is a fallen angel, an angel sent by God, or the same as the “angel of the abyss” in verse 11 is disputed.

The older tradition has “the bottomless pit,” which merges two Greek nouns into one image. The first word means a well or shaft; the second, in the Greek Old Testament, is the deep, and by this period was also used for the underworld prison of evil spirits. The picture is of a locked shaft leading down into that deep. Several modern versions also render it “shaft of the abyss.”

The passive “was given” recurs through the chapter (verses 1, 3, and 5, where it is rendered “permitted”). In Jewish writing this is a reverent way of indicating that God is the one who grants or allows something. The destroyers act only within limits set from above.

The reason for the figure is uncertain. A common suggestion is that it reflects the rough life span or season of natural locusts; others take it simply as a limited period. Either way the point is that the torment has a set end.

Abaddon is a Hebrew word meaning “destruction,” used in the Old Testament as a name for the realm of the dead alongside Sheol. Apollyon is a Greek word meaning “destroyer.” Some scholars hear in the Greek name a jab at the god Apollo, whose name was sometimes linked with the same verb, but this is not certain.

Many manuscripts read “the four horns,” and many English versions follow them. Other early witnesses lack “four,” and the Greek text translated here omits it. The horns are the projections at the corners of the altar, so the sense is unaffected.

In the Old Testament the Euphrates marks the far boundary of the promised land, and the direction from which invading armies of Assyria and Babylon came. In John’s day it was also the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthian cavalry that Rome feared.

notes.phrase: the hour and day and month and year
notes.note: In Greek a single “the” governs all four nouns, so they name one appointed moment rather than four periods of time. The angels have been held for a precise point fixed in advance.

notes.phrase: twice ten thousand times ten thousand
notes.note: Literally “two myriads of myriads,” which works out to two hundred million. The myriad (ten thousand) was the largest number with its own name in Greek, and the expression echoes Old Testament language for countless hosts, so it may be meant as an unimaginably vast number, not an exact count.

notes.phrase: fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow
notes.traditional: of fire, and of jacinth, and brimstone
notes.note: The Greek has three adjectives: “fiery,” “hyacinth-like,” and “sulfurous.” They are usually understood as colors, with “hyacinth” denoting a dark blue or violet like smoke, so that the breastplates match the fire, smoke, and sulfur coming from the horses’ mouths. They could instead describe material or appearance. The Greek also leaves open whether the breastplates belong to the riders alone or to horses and riders together.

Most translations have “repent,” an established term that readers are expected to understand as including a change of life. In current English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and “turn back” is used here to keep that sense.

The Greek word means drugs, potions, or poisons, and by extension the charms and spells that used them. Most translations take it here as magical practice in general. Coming directly after “murders,” it could also be read as “poisonings.” Some manuscripts have the closely related abstract noun for sorcery instead.

Very frequent across the New Testament and split between “authority,” “power” and “right”; here “power” fits a capacity to harm, but the choice should be governed centrally.
Occurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, with renderings ranging from “fornication” to “sexual immorality” to “prostitution,” and its scope is debated.
Means “blow, wound” elsewhere and “plague” throughout Revelation, where it echoes the Exodus plagues; the sense boundary needs one decision.
In Revelation it means “harm, damage,” but elsewhere “wrong, do injustice”; consistency within each sense needs a ruling.
